MathMagic: Comparing and Ordering Fractions

Open the Comparing and Ordering Fractions video
Read the Comparing and Ordering Fractions transcript

Two friends both claim they've chosen the bigger share of the same-sized chocolate bar.

How could a picture settle this delicious disagreement?

Today, we're learning to compare and order fractions, so we can explain which amount is greater, smaller or equal.

You'll compare shares fairly, using wholes of the same size.

You'll use a picture or equivalent fractions to explain your choice, rather than guessing from the numbers.

And you'll put fractions in order by finding their positions on a number line.

First, choose one whole.

Its parts must be equal in size.

The outline of the model shows the entire whole, not just the coloured share.

Here, three equal parts are chosen out of four.

The top number, the numerator, counts chosen parts.

The bottom number, the denominator, tells how many equal parts make the whole.

A fraction starts with equal parts.

Here, one whole is divided into four equal pieces.

Shade three pieces.

The numerator, three, counts the shaded parts.

The denominator, four, counts the equal parts in the whole.

A strip shows the same amount.

Three of four equal lengths are shaded.

The picture changes, but the value stays the same.

Look at these two equal-sized wholes.

Which has the greater coloured share?

Count the quarter-sized pieces before you decide.

When denominators match, the pieces have the same size.

Three quarters is greater than two quarters because three pieces are more than two.

We can count these pieces directly because their sizes match.

With the same denominator and equal-sized wholes, more chosen parts means more of the whole.

Now compare one third and one sixth.

These wholes are the same length, but the sixths are smaller pieces.

So one third is greater than one sixth.

A bigger denominator does not always mean a bigger fraction.

It can be tempting to choose the fraction with the bigger denominator.

But dividing the same whole into more pieces makes each piece smaller, not bigger.

Now the pieces have different sizes.

Predict whether three quarters or one half is greater.

Could you describe the half using quarters?

Return to three quarters and one half.

Split each half into two equal pieces.

One half becomes two quarters.

Only the divisions have changed.

The half still covers exactly the same length.

Two quarters and one half are equivalent names for that amount.

Now the parts match.

Three quarters is greater than two quarters, so three quarters is greater than one half.

A number line shows fraction size as distance from zero.

Divide the distance from zero to one into four equal intervals.

One quarter is one interval from zero.

One half is two intervals, and three quarters is three intervals.

Read from left to right to order them from smallest to largest: one quarter, one half, then three quarters.

Which is greater, five eighths or three eighths?

Five eighths is greater: the same-sized parts are being counted.

Our goal was to compare and order fractions.

You can compare equal parts, explain a fair comparison, and read a number line.

Which model will help you explain your next answer?

Try the practice on Math Magic.

MathMagic: Equivalent Fractions

Open the Equivalent Fractions video
Read the Equivalent Fractions transcript

Can a share change its name without getting any bigger?

Imagine dividing your half of a ribbon into smaller pieces.

Have you somehow gained more ribbon?

Today, we're learning to recognise, create and explain equivalent fractions: different names for exactly the same amount.

You'll recognise equal amounts, even when the pictures have different numbers of pieces.

You'll create a new fraction name by changing both numbers fairly.

You'll also simplify a fraction, and use a model to explain why its value stays the same.

First, choose one whole.

Its parts must be equal in size.

The outline of the model shows the entire whole, not just the coloured share.

Here, three equal parts are chosen out of four.

The top number, the numerator, counts chosen parts.

The bottom number, the denominator, tells how many equal parts make the whole.

If every half is split into two equal pieces, what will happen to the coloured amount?

Predict its new fraction name.

Start with one half.

Split every part of the whole into two equal pieces.

The shaded half now contains two quarters.

Split every quarter in half again.

Now four of eight equal pieces are shaded.

One half, two quarters and four eighths are equivalent.

Notice the coloured length stays fixed while the boundaries change.

We aren't adding ribbon; we're choosing a new way to count equal-sized pieces.

The number rule matches the picture.

Multiply the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number.

Can you give three fifths a new name with twenty equal parts in the whole?

Think about what changes and what must stay unchanged.

For three fifths, multiply both numbers by four.

Three times four is twelve, and five times four is twenty.

The whole has four times as many pieces, and the chosen share has four times as many pieces too.

Changing both counts together keeps the share unchanged.

Equivalent fractions also land at the same point on a number line.

They are different names for one number.

Simplifying works in reverse.

Group equal pieces together instead of splitting them into smaller pieces.

Group the eighths in pairs.

Six eighths becomes three quarters.

We divided the numerator and denominator by two.

Try twelve eighteenths.

Both twelve and eighteen divide by six.

Twelve divided by six is two; eighteen divided by six is three.

Be careful: adding the same number to both numbers does not preserve the value.

One half and two thirds are different amounts.

Adding one to the top and bottom gives two thirds, not another name for one half.

Compare the equal-length bars: the coloured amounts are different.

We can also partition a fraction.

Three quarters is three one-quarter pieces added together.

Two quarters make one half, so three quarters is also one half plus one quarter.

Different partitions can describe the same amount.

Is six eighths equivalent to three quarters?

Yes.

Dividing both six and eight by two gives three quarters.

We set out to recognise, create and explain equivalent fractions.

You can split or group equal parts, change both numbers together, and check that the amount stays the same.

How many names can you find for one half?

Explore the practice on Math Magic.

MathMagic: Mixed Numbers and Improper Fractions

Open the Mixed Numbers and Improper Fractions video
Read the Mixed Numbers and Improper Fractions transcript

Imagine sharing eleven quarter-sized pieces among a group.

Counting pieces is easy, but how many whole units could you build?

There's more than one way to name this amount!

Today, we're learning to represent and convert mixed numbers and improper fractions, without changing the amount they describe.

You'll group equal pieces to see complete wholes and any extra part.

You'll turn an improper fraction into a mixed number, and go back the other way.

You'll check that both names match the same model or number-line position.

First, choose one whole.

Its parts must be equal in size.

The outline of the model shows the entire whole, not just the coloured share.

Here, three equal parts are chosen out of four.

The top number, the numerator, counts chosen parts.

The bottom number, the denominator, tells how many equal parts make the whole.

How many complete wholes can you build from eleven quarters?

Group four pieces at a time, and notice any pieces left over.

Four quarters make one whole.

Another four quarters make a second whole.

Three quarters are left over.

Eleven quarters is an improper fraction.

Its numerator is at least as large as its denominator.

It can describe one whole or more.

Two and three quarters is a mixed number.

It combines two whole units with a fractional part.

To convert, divide eleven by four.

Eleven divided by four is two with a remainder of three.

The denominator stays four because our pieces are still quarters.

So eleven quarters equals two and three quarters.

The remainder counts extra quarter-sized pieces.

It doesn't become the denominator.

A picture helps you see two complete wholes and three quarters of the next one.

How could you count all the fifth-sized pieces in three and two fifths?

Remember that each whole contains five fifths.

Now go the other way.

Take three and two fifths.

Each whole contains five fifths.

Three times five gives fifteen fifths.

Add the extra two fifths to make seventeen fifths.

So three and two fifths equals seventeen fifths.

Multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the denominator.

Counting in fifths doesn't change the whole or the amount.

It simply replaces the whole-number groups with a single count of equal pieces.

A mixed number isn't made by adding its whole number to its numerator.

Two and three quarters is not five quarters.

The two wholes already contain eight quarters.

Eight quarters plus three quarters is eleven quarters.

That's why we multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the extra numerator.

A fraction can also equal an exact whole.

Eight quarters is two wholes, with no fractional part left over.

To compare mixed numbers, compare the wholes first.

Three and one quarter is greater than two and three quarters.

If the wholes match, compare the fractional parts.

Two and one half is greater than two and one quarter.

A number line helps us check amounts beyond one.

Two and one half is ten quarter-steps from zero.

Two and three quarters is one quarter-step further to the right.

How many wholes and quarters are in nine quarters?

Nine quarters is two wholes and one quarter.

Our goal was to connect mixed numbers and improper fractions.

You can build wholes, count the leftover parts, and convert in either direction.

Before calculating, what would your amount look like?

Try drawing it, then practise on Math Magic.

MathMagic: Adding and Subtracting Fractions

Open the Adding and Subtracting Fractions video
Read the Adding and Subtracting Fractions transcript

You're making a snack mix.

One scoop fills half a cup, and another fills a quarter of a cup.

Will they fill the cup, spill over, or leave some space?

Today, we're learning to add and subtract fractions using visual models and number strategies.

The secret is working with equal-sized parts.

You'll make the parts the same size when the denominators are related.

You'll add or subtract carefully, and simplify your answer when you can.

You'll use a model, a number line or an estimate to explain why your answer makes sense.

First, choose one whole.

Its parts must be equal in size.

The outline of the model shows the entire whole, not just the coloured share.

Here, three equal parts are chosen out of four.

The top number, the numerator, counts chosen parts.

The bottom number, the denominator, tells how many equal parts make the whole.

What is two sevenths plus three sevenths?

Think about the size of each piece, then predict the number of pieces altogether.

First, use matching denominators.

Two sevenths plus three sevenths makes five sevenths.

We add the numerators and keep the denominator.

We are still counting sevenths, not fourteenths.

Adding denominators would rename our pieces as fourteenths, even though we never cut the pieces smaller.

Keep the piece size, and count the chosen pieces.

For half a cup plus a quarter of a cup, what size of piece could you use for both amounts?

Predict the total.

For one half plus one quarter, the denominators are related: four is a multiple of two.

Rename the half as two quarters.

Now add two quarters and one quarter.

The result is three quarters.

Two quarters plus one quarter is three quarters.

That's more than half a cup but less than a full cup, which agrees with the picture.

Subtraction follows the same idea.

For three quarters minus one eighth, rename three quarters as six eighths.

Take away one eighth.

Five eighths remain.

The denominator stays eight.

Six eighths with one eighth removed leaves five eighths.

The result is smaller than three quarters, so our subtraction passes a quick sense check.

On a number line, begin at six eighths and move back one eighth.

You land on five eighths.

Simplify when you can.

One sixth plus three sixths is four sixths, which equals two thirds.

Mixed numbers can make another whole.

One and four fifths plus two fifths is one and six fifths.

Regroup five fifths as one whole.

The answer is two and one fifth.

For several fractions, rename them with a common denominator.

One half plus one quarter minus one eighth becomes four eighths plus two eighths minus one eighth.

Four plus two minus one is five, so the result is five eighths.

What is two thirds minus one sixth?

Two thirds is four sixths.

Four sixths minus one sixth is three sixths, or one half.

Our goal was to add and subtract fractions.

Make the parts match, combine or remove them, then simplify and check.

What would you draw first for your next calculation?

Try the fraction practice on Math Magic.

The separate L C M video is optional extension work.

MathMagic: Fraction Word Problems

Open the Fraction Word Problems video
Read the Fraction Word Problems transcript

A recipe, a ribbon and a walking track all hide fraction puzzles.

Your first job isn't to grab the numbers.

It's to discover what the story is really asking!

Today, we're learning to interpret everyday fraction problems, choose a suitable strategy, and explain a solution that makes sense.

You'll identify the whole and the unit, so you know what each fraction describes.

You'll choose an operation and make a model before you calculate.

You'll explain your answer with its unit, then check it against the story.

First, choose one whole.

Its parts must be equal in size.

The outline of the model shows the entire whole, not just the coloured share.

Here, three equal parts are chosen out of four.

The top number, the numerator, counts chosen parts.

The bottom number, the denominator, tells how many equal parts make the whole.

A recipe uses half a cup of oats and a quarter of a cup of nuts.

What operation fits the question: how much altogether?

First identify the whole: one cup.

Altogether tells us to combine the amounts, so choose addition.

Rename one half as two quarters.

Two quarters plus one quarter makes three quarters.

Mia uses three quarters of a cup altogether.

That is more than half a cup and less than one cup, so the answer makes sense.

A useful answer tells the amount and its unit: three quarters of a cup.

Compare it with the ingredients to check that nothing has disappeared or been counted twice.

A ribbon is two metres long.

We cut off three quarters of a metre.

Will the remaining length be more or less than one metre?

Now a ribbon is two metres long.

We cut off three quarters of a metre.

How much ribbon remains?

We want what remains, so subtract.

Two metres equals eight quarter-metres.

Eight quarters minus three quarters is five quarters.

Five quarters is one and one quarter.

One and one quarter metres remain.

On the number line, move back three quarter-steps from two.

The three quarters refers to one metre, not three quarters of the two-metre ribbon.

Naming the unit clearly prevents a very different calculation.

For a comparison, Ava walks three quarters of a kilometre.

Leo walks five eighths of a kilometre.

Who walks farther, and by how much?

Rename three quarters as six eighths.

Ava walks farther because six eighths is greater than five eighths.

Subtract five eighths from six eighths.

Ava walks one eighth of a kilometre farther.

Here is a two-step problem.

A jug holds one litre.

We pour out a quarter of a litre, then another half a litre.

How much remains?

A quarter plus a half is three quarters of a litre poured out.

Subtract three quarters from one whole litre.

One quarter of a litre remains.

Check: three quarters poured out plus one quarter remaining makes one whole litre.

You walk two thirds of a kilometre, then one sixth more.

How far is that altogether?

Two thirds is four sixths.

Adding one sixth gives five sixths of a kilometre.

Our goal was to solve and explain everyday fraction problems.

Identify the whole, model the relationship, calculate and check the unit.

Could you invent a fraction story about your own day?

Give it a try, then explore the practice on Math Magic.

MathMagic: Understanding Place Value

Open the Understanding Place Value lesson video
Read the Understanding Place Value video transcript

Imagine two identical digits applying for different jobs in a giant number.

One earns ten times as much as its neighbour!

How can the very same digit have such different values?

Let’s uncover its place-value secret.

Today, we’re learning to explain how a digit’s place changes its value in a whole number.

You’ll be able to name a digit’s place and give its value.

You’ll be able to use a place-value chart to explain a number.

You’ll be able to explain why the same digit is worth ten times as much one place to the left.

What makes the same digit worth ten times as much?

Its position does.

In our base ten system, ten ones make one ten, and ten tens make one hundred.

Each place is ten times the place immediately to its right.

Look at the seven in this number.

Before I explain, predict which place it holds.

Remember to count from ones at the right.

Look at four hundred and seventy two thousand, six hundred and thirty one.

Put each digit into its own column, from hundred thousands down to ones.

The seven is in the ten thousands column.

Its value is seventy thousand, not seven thousand.

The two stands for two thousand, the six for six hundred, and the three for thirty.

Reading the number in groups helps: four hundred and seventy two thousand, then six hundred and thirty one.

Every digit has a job.

Now look at these two fives.

Which one has the greater value?

Point to its column before we compare.

Now compare the two fives in fifty five thousand.

The first five represents fifty thousand.

The second represents five thousand.

Fifty thousand is ten times five thousand, even though the digits look the same.

This relationship helps us multiply and divide whole numbers by ten.

Thirty four times ten is three hundred and forty.

Each digit takes a place worth ten times as much.

Three hundred and forty divided by ten returns thirty four.

A common mix-up is saying that the seven here is just worth seven.

Seven names the digit, but its column tells us its value.

In the ten-thousands column, it represents seven groups of ten thousand.

In 583,214, what is the value of the eight?

The eight is in the ten-thousands place.

Its value is eighty thousand.

Try the page example: five hundred and eighty three thousand, two hundred and fourteen.

The eight is in the ten thousands place, so it represents eighty thousand.

Remember: name the place first, then work out the value.

One place left means ten times as much.

Our goal was to explain how a digit’s place changes its value in a whole number.

You can now explain your strategy, check the places carefully, and show why your answer makes sense.

Choose a number of your own and explain it to someone nearby.

Then try the lesson practice on Math Magic.

MathMagic: Expanded Form & Representing Numbers

Open the Expanded Form & Representing Numbers lesson video
Read the Expanded Form & Representing Numbers video transcript

A number arrives at a costume party.

Sometimes it wears digits, sometimes words, and sometimes a long addition sentence.

Can we spot the same number beneath every disguise?

Let’s become number detectives.

Today, we’re learning to read, write and regroup a whole number without changing its value.

You’ll be able to match a number to its word form and expanded form.

You’ll be able to explain how zero holds an empty place.

You’ll be able to regroup thousands and hundreds to show the same amount.

How can one number have several correct representations?

We can write its digits, say it in words, or split it into place values.

All three describe the same quantity.

Let us represent four hundred and six thousand, two hundred and seventy five.

How would you describe this number without using its digits?

Notice the empty ten-thousands place before we unpack the number.

Start with the largest place.

The four means four hundred thousand.

The zero ten thousands contributes zero.

The six means six thousand.

Keep that zero as a placeholder when writing the standard number, so every other digit stays in the right place.

Now add the smaller places: two hundred, seventy and five.

The expanded form is four hundred thousand, plus six thousand, plus two hundred, plus seventy, plus five.

We can leave out the zero contribution without changing the total.

In words, say four hundred and six thousand, two hundred and seventy five.

Notice how the thousands group and the final three digits fit together.

The word form, standard form and expanded form all represent four hundred and six thousand, two hundred and seventy five.

Can we describe three thousand four hundred using only hundreds?

Predict how many hundreds would make the same amount.

We can also regroup a number.

Three thousand four hundred is three thousands and four hundreds.

It is also thirty four hundreds, because thirty four groups of one hundred make three thousand four hundred.

The grouping changes; the amount does not.

It is tempting to erase the zero when writing the number in digits.

But removing that placeholder shifts the other digits into different places.

Leave zero in the standard number, even when its zero contribution is omitted from expanded form.

What number is six hundred thousand plus twenty thousand plus four thousand plus three hundred plus eight?

The total is six hundred and twenty-four thousand, three hundred and eight.

There are zero tens.

For practice, combine six hundred thousand, twenty thousand, four thousand, three hundred and eight.

That gives six hundred and twenty four thousand, three hundred and eight.

There are no tens, but the zero still holds their place.

Remember: read, partition and regroup, while keeping the value unchanged.

Our goal was to read, write and regroup a whole number without changing its value.

You can now explain your strategy, check the places carefully, and show why your answer makes sense.

Choose a number of your own and explain it to someone nearby.

Then try the lesson practice on Math Magic.

MathMagic: Comparing & Ordering Whole Numbers

Open the Comparing & Ordering Whole Numbers lesson video
Read the Comparing & Ordering Whole Numbers video transcript

Two friends are checking numbered tickets for a school event.

Almost every digit matches!

Which ticket comes first?

A quick glance at the final digits could fool us, so let’s investigate from the right starting place.

Today, we’re learning to compare and order whole numbers using place value.

You’ll be able to compare from the largest place until I find a difference.

You’ll be able to use the symbols <, > and = correctly.

You’ll be able to order numbers and explain your choice using digit values.

Which number is larger when most of the digits match?

Compare from the greatest place value, not from the right.

For whole numbers with no leading zeros, more digits means a larger number.

If the lengths match, compare one column at a time.

Which ticket number is greater?

Point to the first place where the digits differ.

We can stop once we find it.

Compare four hundred and fifty six thousand, seven hundred and eighty two, with four hundred and fifty six thousand, seven hundred and twenty eight.

Their hundred thousands, ten thousands, thousands and hundreds match.

We have not found a difference yet, so keep moving right.

At the tens place, eight is greater than two.

Stop there.

The first number is greater, so four hundred and fifty six thousand, seven hundred and eighty two is greater than four hundred and fifty six thousand, seven hundred and twenty eight.

The ones cannot overturn that difference.

Try this pair before I show the comparison.

Will the many nines at the end decide the answer, or will an earlier place decide?

Now compare three hundred and nine thousand, nine hundred and fifty, with three hundred and ten thousand and five.

The hundred thousands match.

At ten thousands, zero is less than one.

Therefore three hundred and nine thousand, nine hundred and fifty is smaller.

To order several numbers, repeat the same method.

Eighty nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety nine comes before ninety thousand and one, which comes before ninety thousand and ten.

Do not compare only the final three digits.

The greatest differing place decides.

Sam compares only the final three digits and thinks eighty-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine must be greater than ninety thousand and one.

That overlooks the ten-thousands!

Nine ten-thousands is greater than eight ten-thousands, whatever follows.

Which is greater: 582,430 or 582,403?

The first differing place is the tens.

Three tens is greater than zero tens, so 582,430 is greater.

As a supporting estimation check, rounding eighty nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety nine to the nearest thousand gives ninety thousand.

A rounded value is useful, but it does not replace an exact comparison.

Recap: line up the places, start left, find the first difference, and explain your order.

Our goal was to compare and order whole numbers using place value.

You can now explain your strategy, check the places carefully, and show why your answer makes sense.

Choose a number of your own and explain it to someone nearby.

Then try the lesson practice on Math Magic.

MathMagic: Decimal Place Value

Open the Decimal Place Value lesson video
Read the Decimal Place Value video transcript

Imagine a measuring strip that keeps zooming in.

First we see little parts, then even smaller parts inside those.

How can we name an amount precisely?

Our place-value pattern has a wonderfully useful answer.

Today, we’re learning to explain decimal place value through thousandths.

You’ll be able to name tenths, hundredths and thousandths.

You’ll be able to give a decimal digit’s value and write a number in expanded form.

You’ll be able to explain the ten-times relationship between neighbouring places.

What happens when we split one whole into smaller equal parts?

The same base ten pattern continues beyond the decimal point.

After ones come tenths, hundredths and thousandths.

Each place is one tenth of the value of the place immediately to its left.

Before we name each part, predict the value of the seven.

Is it seven wholes, seven tenths, or seven hundredths?

Read four point seven two six.

The four is four ones.

The seven is seven tenths, written zero point seven.

The two is two hundredths, written zero point zero two.

The six is six thousandths, written zero point zero zero six.

Put the parts together.

Four point seven two six equals four, plus zero point seven, plus zero point zero two, plus zero point zero zero six.

The digits describe different sized parts, so their positions matter just as much as they do in whole numbers.

The digit five appears in both numbers.

Do you think these two amounts are equal?

Picture tenths and hundredths before deciding.

A tenth is ten hundredths.

A hundredth is ten thousandths.

Now compare zero point five with zero point zero five.

Five tenths is ten times five hundredths, so zero point five is greater.

The same digit does not mean the same value.

Think of a measuring scale marked in equal small steps.

Thousandths let us describe positions more precisely than hundredths.

This is about understanding place value, not just counting how many digits come after the point.

Keep the whole and the size of each part clear.

A five after one decimal place and a five after two decimal places do not have the same value.

Five tenths is ten times five hundredths.

Keep the same-sized whole in mind when you compare the parts.

What is the value of the eight in 5.218?

The eight is in the thousandths place, so it represents eight thousandths.

Try the page example: three point four five eight.

The five is in the hundredths place, so its value is zero point zero five.

Remember: ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

Every step right divides the place value by ten; every step left makes it ten times as much.

Our goal was to explain decimal place value through thousandths.

You can now explain your strategy, check the places carefully, and show why your answer makes sense.

Choose a number of your own and explain it to someone nearby.

Then try the lesson practice on Math Magic.

MathMagic: Compare, Order & Locate Decimals

Open the Compare, Order & Locate Decimals lesson video
Read the Compare, Order & Locate Decimals video transcript

Two measuring displays disagree about who has the bigger amount.

One display has more digits, but does that make its amount greater?

Let’s use matching places and a zoomable number line to solve the mystery.

Today, we’re learning to compare, order and locate decimals through thousandths.

You’ll be able to line up places and use end zeros without changing a decimal’s value.

You’ll be able to compare and order decimals using place value.

You’ll be able to explain where a decimal belongs between two number-line marks.

Does a longer decimal always mean a bigger number?

No.

Compare place values instead.

Start with the whole number parts, then tenths, hundredths and thousandths.

Adding zeros at the end of a decimal can help line up the places without changing its value.

Which display shows the greater amount?

Try matching the decimal places, rather than counting how many digits you see.

Compare one point four zero seven and one point four seven.

Write the second as one point four seven zero.

Ones and tenths match.

At the hundredths place, zero is less than seven.

So one point four zero seven is less than one point four seven zero.

For ordering, line up two point zero five three, two point three zero five, and two point three five zero.

The first is smallest because its tenths digit is zero.

The other two match in tenths, but zero hundredths is less than five hundredths.

Where might one point four three seven lie?

First find its neighbouring hundredths.

Then we can zoom in together.

Now locate a number on a line.

From one point four zero to one point five zero, divide the interval into ten equal steps.

Each step is one hundredth.

One point four three and one point four four are neighbouring marks on this line.

To locate one point four three seven more precisely, zoom in between one point four three and one point four four.

Divide that interval into ten equal steps.

Each step is one thousandth.

Count seven steps from one point four three zero to reach one point four three seven.

A longer decimal is not automatically larger.

One point four zero seven is smaller than one point four seven.

Adding an end zero to make one point four seven zero changes its name, but not its value.

Which is greater: 2.405 or 2.45?

Write 2.45 as 2.450.

At the hundredths place, five hundredths is greater than zero hundredths.

Finally, four point seven equals four point seven zero zero: both represent seven tenths after four wholes.

Extra end zeros do not add any value.

Remember: line up the places, compare from the left, and check the equal step size before locating a decimal.

Our goal was to compare, order and locate decimals through thousandths.

You can now explain your strategy, check the places carefully, and show why your answer makes sense.

Choose a number of your own and explain it to someone nearby.

Then try the lesson practice on Math Magic.

MathMagic: Connect Fractions, Decimals and Percentages

Open the Connect Fractions, Decimals and Percentages video
Read the video transcript

Can one amount have three different mathematical names? Today we are connecting fractions, decimals and percentages. We will use the same whole each time, rename shares in hundredths, and explain why the notation changes while the amount stays the same.

Our learning goal is to connect familiar fractions, decimals and percentages that represent the same amount.

Success criteria. I can match familiar fractions to equivalent decimals and percentages. I can use a visual model to explain why the forms are equivalent. I can place equivalent representations at the same position on a number line.

A fraction describes equal parts, a decimal uses place-value parts, and a percentage uses hundredths. Rename a familiar fraction in hundredths to connect all three. Always keep the whole unchanged.

One half of a whole is fifty hundredths. In decimal notation that is zero point five zero, or zero point five.

Fifty hundredths is fifty percent. All three names identify the midpoint between zero and one, so the amount has not changed.

Three quarters is seventy-five hundredths. In decimal notation it is zero point seven five.

Seventy-five hundredths is seventy-five percent. One quarter would be twenty-five hundredths, or zero point two five, or twenty-five percent.

One fifth is how many tenths, and what decimal and percentage does it represent?

One fifth is two tenths, or twenty hundredths. That gives zero point two and twenty percent.

Keep the same whole and connect through equal parts. One half, one quarter, three quarters, one tenth and one fifth are useful benchmarks. Equivalent representations locate the same amount on a number line.

Our learning goal is to measure mass and capacity using scales and combined units.

Success criteria. I can distinguish mass from capacity. I can read equal scale intervals. I can combine kilograms and grams or litres and millilitres.

Mass describes how heavy an object is; capacity describes how much a container can hold. Use grams or kilograms for mass, and millilitres or litres for capacity. One kilogram is one thousand grams. One litre is one thousand millilitres. On every scale, count equal intervals before deciding what one interval represents.

A bag has a mass of one kilogram and three hundred and fifty grams. Picture one thousand grams as a whole kilogram, with the smaller amount added alongside. What single gram reading would describe the same mass?

One thousand plus three hundred and fifty is one thousand three hundred and fifty grams. The bag has not become heavier because we changed its name. Kilograms and grams are two units for the same attribute.

A jug holds two litres and two hundred and fifty millilitres. Convert the whole litres first. Two groups of one thousand millilitres make two thousand millilitres. Then include the extra marked amount.

The capacity is two thousand two hundred and fifty millilitres. On a scale from zero to one thousand with four equal intervals, each interval would be two hundred and fifty millilitres. Count intervals, not just tick marks.

Grams and millilitres are not interchangeable labels. A balance measures mass; a marked jug measures capacity. Equal numerical readings do not make those attributes the same. Read the instrument and include the correct unit.

A balance points halfway between five hundred and six hundred grams. What mass does it show? Look at the model, and keep your prediction in mind.

Halfway is fifty grams beyond five hundred, giving five hundred and fifty grams. The scale is measuring mass, so the answer needs grams, not millilitres.

Choose the attribute, unit and instrument together. For a practical challenge, use a kitchen balance or marked jug with an adult. Predict a reading, measure carefully, and explain the difference between your estimate and observation. Reflect on which model helped you and why. Now try the MathMagic practice, and explain your thinking to someone.

MathMagic: Trace and Calculate Perimeter

Open the Trace and Calculate Perimeter video
Read the video transcript

A school garden needs a fence. Would counting the squares inside tell us how much fencing to buy? Imagine walking all the way around its edge. That journey measures the boundary, which is called the perimeter.

Our learning goal is to find the perimeter of regular and irregular shapes.

Success criteria. I can trace the complete outside boundary. I can use matching length units. I can find missing lengths before adding sides.

Use string to trace a shape, then straighten the string beside a ruler. This makes the idea of perimeter concrete. On a diagram, follow every outside side once and add those lengths using matching units. An inside dividing line is not part of the outside boundary.

A rectangular garden is seven metres long and four metres wide. Opposite sides have matching lengths. Trace the four edges and predict the total before we add them.

Seven plus four plus seven plus four is twenty-two metres. We can also add seven and four, then double eleven. Both methods count the complete boundary exactly once.

Now trace an L-shaped garden. Its top is eight metres and its left side is six. A three-by-two rectangle is missing from the lower right corner. Use subtraction to find the remaining straight lengths.

The six outside edges measure eight, four, three, two, five and six metres. Their sum is twenty-eight metres. The inward corner still belongs to the outside boundary, so include both of its edges.

Seven times four counts square units covering this rectangle. It does not measure the fence. For perimeter, trace and add the outside lengths. A useful check is whether your answer has metres or square metres.

A rectangle is six metres by three metres. What is its perimeter? Look at the model, and keep your prediction in mind.

Six plus three makes nine. Double nine for the four sides: eighteen metres. Check by tracing and adding six, three, six and three.

Perimeter is a length around the complete outside edge. Trace before calculating, find hidden lengths and keep units consistent. Try outlining a book with string, then compare a direct measurement with the total of its side lengths. Reflect on which model helped you and why. Now try the MathMagic practice, and explain your thinking to someone.

MathMagic: Cover and Calculate Area

Open the Cover and Calculate Area video
Read the video transcript

How many equal square tiles would cover a small floor? A long piece of string cannot cover the surface. We need a different measure from perimeter: area tells us how much flat space a shape covers.

Our learning goal is to explain and find area using square units.

Success criteria. I can cover a surface without gaps or overlaps. I can use rows and columns to count squares. I can distinguish area from perimeter.

Arrange equal unit squares without gaps or overlaps. Each square covers one square unit. For a rectangle, equal rows let us count efficiently with multiplication. A square centimetre is a square one centimetre along each side, not a one-centimetre length.

A rectangle has eight columns and five rows of square-centimetre tiles. Predict how many unit squares cover it. Each row contains eight squares, and there are five equal rows.

Five groups of eight make forty unit squares. The area is forty square centimetres. Multiplying eight centimetres by five centimetres counts the same tiled surface, so we write the squared unit.

A play mat is seven metres by four metres. Imagine covering it with one-metre squares. There are seven squares along each row, with four rows altogether. What would the surface measurement be?

The area is twenty-eight square metres. The perimeter is a different quantity: seven plus four plus seven plus four is twenty-two metres. Area counts the cover; perimeter measures the border.

Adding eight and five does not count the tiles covering an eight-by-five rectangle. It counts only two side lengths. To find area, use all five rows of eight equal squares, with no gaps or overlaps.

A rectangle has six columns and four rows of unit squares. What is its area? Look at the model, and keep your prediction in mind.

Four groups of six make twenty-four square units. You can check by counting the tiles or adding six four times. No tile should be counted twice.

Area counts equal squares covering a surface. Use rows and columns to count efficiently and always label the square unit. Draw two rectangles with the same area on squared paper. Do they have to have the same perimeter? Explain with a drawing. Reflect on which model helped you and why. Now try the MathMagic practice, and explain your thinking to someone.

MathMagic: Design with Irregular Shapes

Open the Design with Irregular Shapes video
Read the video transcript

A playground has a corner cut out for a tree. Can we still work out how many paving tiles it needs? An irregular outline does not stop us measuring. Let us turn the tricky shape into familiar rectangles.

Our learning goal is to solve practical problems with irregular shapes.

Success criteria. I can split a shape or subtract a missing rectangle. I can check every outside length for perimeter. I can compare designs using the required measure.

Build an L shape with square tiles, then slide a pencil along possible dividing lines. You can split its area into non-overlapping rectangles, or start with a large rectangle and subtract the missing part. Both methods must cover exactly the same surface.

An L-shaped space fits inside an eight-metre by six-metre rectangle. A three-metre by two-metre corner is missing. Predict whether its area is greater or smaller than forty-eight square metres.

Subtract the missing six square metres from forty-eight. The L-shaped area is forty-two square metres. As a check, split it into an eight-by-four rectangle and a five-by-two rectangle. Thirty-two plus ten also gives forty-two.

A larger design fits inside a ten-metre by eight-metre rectangle, with a four-by-three corner missing. Plan the area calculation first. Keep the border measurement separate from the surface measurement.

The usable area is sixty-eight square metres. For its border, trace ten, five, four, three, six and eight metres. That perimeter is thirty-six metres. Different questions about the same design need different measures.

Using the full eight-by-six rectangle would include the tree corner. That overcounts six square metres. Subtract the missing rectangle, or add two rectangles that cover only the actual playground.

A six-by-five rectangle has a two-by-two corner removed. What area remains? Look at the model, and keep your prediction in mind.

Thirty minus four leaves twenty-six square units. The missing corner is not part of the surface, so subtract it once, rather than including the full bounding rectangle.

Choose the measure the problem needs. For area, split or subtract rectangles; for perimeter, trace every outside edge. Draw a garden on squared paper and explain a paving plan and a fencing plan. Check that your answers describe the actual design. Reflect on which model helped you and why. Now try the MathMagic practice, and explain your thinking to someone.
